title.narrative: A toolkit for promoting localized Human ‎Security Approaches

description.narrative: The programme aims to provide vulnerable local communities and populations in Lebanon with ‎tools and mechanisms anchored in the human security approach that will enable them to ‎collectively identify and define their own urgent needs, and to engage directly with local ‎authorities and other aid and service providers to respond to their needs, through promoted ‎local dialogue and accountability. Through the human security approach, the programme will ‎increase the resilience of the communities living in the most vulnerable areas of cities and towns. ‎It will be implemented through joining efforts and experiences and by capitalizing on UN-‎Habitat’s expertise in areas of municipal governance and evidence-based planning, on UN ‎Women’s expertise in the delivery of protection services and gender-responsive programming, ‎and UNICEF’s expertise on child protection. The proposed programme will target vulnerable host ‎and refugee populations residing in marginalized areas, specifically women, youth and children ‎with increased multidimensional vulnerabilities, low levels of inclusion in society, high levels of ‎stress, low self-esteem, and heightened sense of insecurity. The goal of the programme is to meet ‎the urgent needs of vulnerable populations in response to Lebanon’s multilayered humanitarian ‎crisis exacerbated by the increased devaluation of the local currency, growing inflation, and high ‎unemployment, pushing hundreds of thousands of families below the poverty line. ‎ The protracted and widening political instability in the country, coupled with an unprecedented ‎financial crisis that has led to a bankrupted national government, has put huge pressure on local ‎actors and communities. Municipalities and local communities are developing and using context-‎specific coping mechanisms that rely on local human, physical and financial resources. The ‎programme will adopt human security approaches by proposing structured approaches and tools ‎that would enable local communities to become agents of change. ‎ The aforementioned strategy/approach is based on the experience previously and recently ‎gained by the three United Nations agencies through Abjad and Markazouna centres in Tripoli, ‎North Lebanon. These two multiservice community-led centres were established as part of ‎multiple rounds of financial assistance provided through the United Nations Trust Fund for ‎Human Security (UNTFHS) since 2017. The two initiatives adopted a localized human security ‎approach that responded to marginalised communities exposed to vulnerability‎’ changing needs ‎and priorities in a flexible and realistic manner, capitalizing on existing local resources. ‎ Human security principles underlie the proposed programme because the approach is people ‎centred, providing concrete and sustainable benefits to people. It is context specific, as it ‎targets and tailors responses to the needs of communities exposed to threats to their ‎livelihoods, survival and dignity. Moreover, the approach focuses on partnering and ‎coordinating with different stakeholders and local communities, thereby building and ‎strengthening cooperative strategic linkages. ‎ Building on the successful results and lessons learned of the previous programmes implemented ‎by the three United Nations agencies, the proposed programme aims to develop and promote a ‎toolkit that involves localized participatory multisectoral planning and implementation options ‎and scenarios that enable local communities in urban settings to work jointly and collectively to ‎respond to emerging needs and priorities. This will allow community groups to define their ‎human security needs and priorities, and to jointly identify suitable solutions that could be ‎realistically addressed, relying on available resources and coping strategies.‎ The approach engages a wide variety of stakeholders actively present in a certain community. ‎This includes firstly host and refugee members of local communities, local authorities such as ‎municipalities, local representation of relevant ministries, aid entities (United Nations, ‎international and national non-governmental organizations [NGOs]), local and grassroots civil ‎society organizations, academia, and the private sector. The toolkit will detail the different roles ‎and ‎ responsibilities of each actor and how they should engage with other counterparts to synergize ‎their interventions and ensure comprehensive response processes. ‎
